A.explanation: From $V = IR$, $1 \text{A} \times 1 \Omega = 1 \text{V}$, so $\text{A}\Omega$ is a valid unit of potential difference.

B.explanation: Potential difference is energy per charge, $V = W/Q$, with unit $\text{J C}^{-1} = \text{N m C}^{-1}$, not $\text{N m}^{-1}\text{C}^{-1}$.

C.explanation: From $P = VI$, $V = P/I$, so $1 \text{W A}^{-1} = 1 \text{V}$, which is a valid unit.

D.explanation: From $P = V^2/R$, $V = \sqrt{PR}$, so $(\Omega \text{W})^{\frac{1}{2}}$ equals the volt and is valid.

hints: Recall what potential difference means in words: energy transferred per unit charge, $V = W/Q$.
Write the base electrical relations $V = IR$ and $P = VI$ and rearrange each to make $V$ the subject.
Compare $\text{N m C}^{-1}$ from $\text{J C}^{-1}$ with the $\text{N m}^{-1}\text{C}^{-1}$ shown in one option and decide which power of metre is required.
walkthrough: Start from the definition: potential difference $V = W/Q$, so $1 \text{V} = 1 \text{J C}^{-1} = 1 \text{N m C}^{-1}$ because $1 \text{J} = 1 \text{N m}$.
Check $\text{A}\Omega$: using $V = IR$, units give $\text{A} \times \Omega$, so this combination equals the volt.
Check $\text{W A}^{-1}$: using $P = VI$, then $V = P/I$, so units give $\text{W}$ divided by $\text{A}$, which also equals the volt.
Check $(\Omega \text{W})^{\frac{1}{2}}$: using $P = V^2/R$, then $V^2 = PR$ and $V = \sqrt{PR}$, so units give $(\Omega \times \text{W})^{\frac{1}{2}}$, which also equals the volt.
The remaining combination $\text{N m}^{-1}\text{C}^{-1}$ has $\text{m}^{-1}$ instead of $\text{m}$, so it equals $\text{J m}^{-2}\text{C}^{-1}$ and cannot equal $\text{J C}^{-1}$. This is option B.
